search-color.title: Find something red
search-color.goal: Recognise colours and name them while moving around the house.
materials: 4 to 6 large colourful objects (clothes, plastic cups, cushions)
steps: Leave several objects of different colours in plain sight in one room.
Show your child something red and say: “Can you bring me something red like this?”
When they bring it, name the colour and the object together.
Repeat with another colour for as long as they enjoy it.
variants: Easier: look for just one colour and leave that object in plain sight.
Harder: ask for two things at once, such as “something blue and something yellow”.
search-color.safety: Use objects bigger than your child's mouth and keep the way clear so they don't trip.

search-soft.title: Soft treasure
search-soft.goal: Explore textures with the hands and learn the words soft and hard.
materials: Soft things from home (towel, cuddly toy, cushion)
Hard, safe things (plastic cup, wooden spoon, box)
steps: Touch a towel with your child and say slowly: “soft”.
Touch a wooden spoon and say: “hard”.
Ask them to bring you something soft from the room.
Then ask for something hard, and compare the two with your hands.
variants: Easier: put three things on the floor and let them pick the soft one.
Harder: add other words such as rough, smooth or squishy.
search-soft.safety: Choose objects with no loose parts or sharp edges, and bigger than your child's mouth.

search-hidden-toy.title: Where is Teddy?
search-hidden-toy.goal: Practise attention and understand that things are still there even when out of sight.
materials: A big toy they love (a teddy bear, a big toy car, a doll)
A blanket or a large box
steps: Show them the toy and say it is going to hide.
Hide it under a blanket while they watch, and ask: “Where is it?”
When they find it, celebrate calmly and choose a new hiding place.
Then hide it while they cover their eyes, always leaving part of it showing.
variants: Easier: leave a paw or a wheel sticking out.
Harder: give word clues: “it's near the door”, “it's under something soft”.
search-hidden-toy.safety: Hide the toy only in low places within reach, never in wardrobes, drawers or on high furniture.

search-odd-one.title: Which one is different?
search-odd-one.goal: Notice details to find the one that is different, just like the game “Odd one out”.
materials: 3 matching objects and 1 different one (for example, three wooden spoons and a plastic cup)
steps: Line up three matching objects and one different one.
Ask: “Which one is not the same?”
When they point to it, ask how it is different.
Mix up the order and change the odd one out.
variants: Easier: make the odd one very different, like a sock among three cups.
Harder: use four nearly identical objects that only differ in colour or size.
search-odd-one.safety: Use only plastic, wooden or fabric objects that won't break and are bigger than your child's mouth.

sort-socks.title: Sock pairs
sort-socks.goal: Find matching pairs and remember where each one is, just like the Memory game.
materials: 5 or 6 pairs of clean socks, ideally in different colours or patterns
steps: Mix the socks up on the floor or on the bed.
Pick one and ask: “Where is its partner?”
When they find it, put the pair together and set it aside.
Keep going until no sock is left alone.
variants: Easier: start with only three very different pairs.
Harder: lay the socks face down in a row and turn over two at a time, like in Memory.
sort-socks.safety: Use clean socks with no decorations that could be pulled off.

sort-colors.title: Each colour to its basket
sort-colors.goal: Group objects by colour and start sorting.
materials: 2 or 3 baskets or boxes
Large objects in those colours (clothes, big toys, plastic cups)
steps: Put each basket on the floor with a sample object inside: one red, one blue.
Gather the other objects in a pile.
Ask them to take each thing to the basket of its colour.
When you finish, check each basket together and name the colours.
variants: Easier: use only two very different colours.
Harder: add a third colour, or sort by type (clothes, toys, kitchen).
sort-colors.safety: Use objects bigger than your child's mouth and low baskets that are light to move.

sort-sizes.title: Big, medium and small
sort-sizes.goal: Compare sizes and put things in order from biggest to smallest.
materials: 3 to 5 plastic cups, tumblers or containers in different sizes
steps: Put the containers on the table or floor, all mixed up.
Show them the biggest and the smallest, and name them.
Ask them to line them up from biggest to smallest.
Then let them nest one inside the other.
variants: Easier: use just two containers, one big and one small.
Harder: ask them to put a toy or a car of the right size inside each container.
sort-sizes.safety: Use only plastic containers, never glass or ceramic.

sort-shadows.title: Torch shadows
sort-shadows.goal: Match each object to its silhouette, just like the Shadows game.
materials: A torch (flashlight)
3 or 4 big toys with clear shapes (animals, a car, a doll)
A plain wall and a dim room
steps: Dim the lights and sit facing a plain wall.
Hold the torch and place a toy in front of it so its shadow appears.
Hide the toy behind you, make the shadow again and ask: “Whose shadow is this?”
Let them find it among the toys and hold it in the light to check.
variants: Easier: keep the toys in view and let them choose between just two.
Harder: make animal shadows with your hands and let them guess which one.
sort-shadows.safety: You always hold the torch: don't let your child play with it or its battery cover.

move-tape-line.title: Tape path
move-tape-line.goal: Improve balance and body control by walking along a line.
materials: Painter's tape or wide masking tape
A clear space on the floor
steps: Stick a straight line on the floor, about two or three long steps long.
Walk along it first yourself, slowly, with your arms out.
Invite them to walk on the line without stepping off.
Once they manage, add a curve or a zigzag.
variants: Easier: make it short and wide, with two strips of tape side by side.
Harder: walk on tiptoes, backwards, or push a toy car along the line as if it were a road.
move-tape-line.safety: Stick the tape away from furniture corners and remove it yourself afterwards; never on skin or near the mouth.

move-cushion-jumps.title: Cushion hop
move-cushion-jumps.goal: Practise jumping, balance and coordination safely.
materials: 3 or 4 big cushions
A clear space on the floor
steps: Lay the cushions on the floor in a path, a little apart.
Show them how to go from one to the next with a big step or a small hop.
Hold their hand the first few times.
Sing a song and let them hop to the beat of the music.
variants: Easier: put the cushions close together so they just walk across.
Harder: space them a bit further apart, or call out a colour and let them hop to that cushion.
move-cushion-jumps.safety: Play only on the floor, away from furniture corners, and never climbing onto the sofa or bed.

move-blanket-tunnel.title: Sheet tunnel
move-blanket-tunnel.goal: Crawl and move through a new space, building confidence and coordination.
materials: A sheet or light blanket
Two sturdy chairs or the back of the sofa
steps: Drape a sheet over two chairs to make a short tunnel, open at both ends.
Go to the other end and call their name.
Let them crawl through until they reach you.
Do it again, now with a cuddly toy waiting at the end.
variants: Easier: lift the sheet with your hands so they can see the way out.
Harder: ask them to carry a cuddly toy through without dropping it.
move-blanket-tunnel.safety: Use a light fabric, always leave both ends open and check that the chairs can't tip over.

move-animal-walk.title: Walk like an animal
move-animal-walk.goal: Move the body in different ways and link each animal to its movement and sound.
materials: Nothing, just some clear space
steps: Pick an animal and show how it moves: a duck, a cat, a frog.
Move around the room together like that animal.
Add the animal's sound as you go.
Let them choose the next animal.
variants: Easier: use only two animals and move slowly.
Harder: play music and, when it stops, name a new animal to change the way you walk.
move-animal-walk.safety: Clear toys off the floor and stay away from furniture corners and stairs.

art-tape-shapes.title: Tape shapes
art-tape-shapes.goal: Get to know basic shapes like circle, square and triangle.
materials: Painter's tape or coloured tape
A large sheet of paper or a table
steps: Make a big square with tape on the paper or the table.
Trace the sides with their finger and count them together.
Make a triangle and ask how it is the same and how it is different.
Offer some ready-cut strips of tape so they can make their own shape.
variants: Easier: make the shapes yourself and let them put a toy inside each one.
Harder: stick the shapes on the floor and name one for them to jump into.
art-tape-shapes.safety: You cut the tape; the strips go on paper or the table, never on skin or near the mouth.

art-paper-tear.title: Tear and stick paper
art-paper-tear.goal: Strengthen the fingers and create a picture of their own with pieces of paper.
materials: Tissue paper, kitchen paper or old magazines
A large sheet of paper
Sticky tape or a child-safe glue stick
steps: Show them how to tear the paper with both hands into big pieces.
Tear a pile of colourful pieces together.
Stick a strip of tape sticky side up, or spread the glue on the sheet yourself.
Let them stick the pieces wherever they like, and give their picture a name.
variants: Easier: just tear, without sticking, for the fun of the sound and the movement.
Harder: draw a simple outline, like a tree, and let them fill it with paper.
art-paper-tear.safety: No scissors for the child: paper is torn by hand, and pick up small scraps so they don't go in the mouth.

art-water-paint.title: Painting with water
art-water-paint.goal: Explore drawing strokes and hand movement without any mess.
materials: A wide paintbrush or a big sponge
A little water in a plastic cup
Dark card or a dark paving stone outside
steps: Pour a little water into the cup, just a finger deep.
Dip the brush and paint a line: the drawing shows up dark.
Give them the brush and let them paint freely.
Watch together as the drawing fades while it dries, and paint again.
variants: Easier: let them paint with wet fingers.
Harder: paint a shape or a letter and let them trace over it with the brush.
art-water-paint.safety: Use very little water, stay right next to your child and dry the floor afterwards so nobody slips.

art-sock-puppet.title: Sock puppet
art-sock-puppet.goal: Create a character and give it a voice, to imagine and express feelings.
materials: A large clean sock
A washable marker (for the adult)
steps: Let them choose a sock and decide which animal or character it will be.
Draw the eyes and mouth yourself with the marker.
Put the sock on your hand and make it say hello in a funny voice.
Hand them the puppet and let them invent a name and a voice.
variants: Easier: you move the puppet and it just asks simple questions.
Harder: make two puppets and let them have a little conversation.
art-sock-puppet.safety: Don't glue on eyes, beads or decorations: draw the face so there are no parts that could come loose.

language-spoon-story.title: Spoon story
language-spoon-story.goal: Make up and tell a simple story with characters made from spoons.
materials: 2 or 3 large wooden spoons
A tea towel as the stage
steps: Introduce each spoon as a character: “This is Grandma Spoon.”
Start a short story: “One day, Grandma Spoon went for a walk…”
Ask what happens next and follow their idea.
End the story with all the characters going to sleep under the tea towel.
variants: Easier: use just one spoon that says hello, eats and goes to sleep.
Harder: let them tell the story while you only ask questions.
language-spoon-story.safety: Use large, smooth wooden spoons with no splinters, and avoid metal cutlery with an edge.

language-what-for.title: What is it for?
language-what-for.goal: Grow vocabulary and understand what each everyday thing is used for.
materials: 4 or 5 safe everyday objects (hairbrush, wooden spoon, towel, shoe, big comb)
steps: Put the objects in front of them, one at a time.
Ask: “What is this? What is it for?”
If they don't know, mime using it and let them copy you.
At the end, ask the other way round: “What do we brush our hair with?”
variants: Easier: you say what it is for and they point to the object.
Harder: ask where each thing is kept and let them take it there.
language-what-for.safety: Use objects with no sharp edges or cords, and none small enough to fit in the mouth.

language-mystery-bag.title: The mystery bag
language-mystery-bag.goal: Recognise objects by touch and describe them with words.
materials: A cloth bag or a pillowcase
3 or 4 familiar, large objects (cuddly toy, wooden spoon, sock, soft ball)
steps: Put one object in the pillowcase without them seeing it.
Let them reach in and feel it without looking.
Ask: “Is it soft or hard? Big or small? What is it?”
Take the object out to check, and swap it for another one.
variants: Easier: show them the objects first and let them guess which one they touched.
Harder: let them describe the object without saying its name while you guess.
language-mystery-bag.safety: Always use a cloth bag or a pillowcase, never a plastic bag, and put it away afterwards.

language-sounds.title: What sounds like this?
language-sounds.goal: Listen carefully and link each sound to the object that makes it.
materials: A pot, a lid and a wooden spoon
2 or 3 plastic containers
steps: Tap the pot with the spoon and let them listen to the sound.
Try the lid and a plastic container, and compare how they sound.
Turn your back, make a sound and ask: “What sounds like this?”
Finish by making music together, loud and then very soft.
variants: Easier: make the sound while they watch and let them point to the object.
Harder: imitate animal sounds and let them guess which one.
language-sounds.safety: Use only cold pots and plastic containers, never glass, and don't put anything small inside to make shakers.

routine-toy-home.title: Every toy to its home
routine-toy-home.goal: Learn to tidy up and that everything has its place, just like the game “To its place”.
materials: 2 or 3 boxes or baskets (one for cuddly toys, one for cars, one for big blocks)
steps: Put a sample in each box: a cuddly toy, a car.
Say: “The toys are going home to sleep.”
Hand them the toys one at a time and let them take each to its box.
When you finish, check each box together and thank them.
variants: Easier: use just one box for everything.
Harder: put a picture on each box and let them tidy up on their own by looking at the picture.
routine-toy-home.safety: Use light boxes without heavy lids that could close on their fingers.

routine-laundry.title: Laundry helper
routine-laundry.goal: Join in with housework and practise sorting by person or by type.
materials: Clean, dry clothes (socks, T-shirts, towels)
A laundry basket
steps: Put the clean clothes on the floor or the bed.
Ask them to find all their own clothes first.
Then let them put socks and towels into piles.
Carry each pile to its place together.
variants: Easier: let them just take the towels out of the basket.
Harder: let them fold a small towel in half, with your help.
routine-laundry.safety: Use only clean, dry clothes, away from the washing machine, the iron and cleaning products.

routine-table.title: Setting the table
routine-table.goal: Count, match and feel part of the family by helping to set the table.
materials: Plastic plates, cups and spoons (unbreakable)
Cloth or paper napkins
steps: Count together how many people are eating.
Hand them the plates one at a time and let them put one at each place.
Then the cups, then the spoons and the napkins.
When everyone sits down, tell them who set the table.
variants: Easier: let them put out only the napkins.
Harder: let them give each person their own colour, or count aloud while handing things out.
routine-table.safety: Use only unbreakable things, with no knives, glass or hot plates.

routine-shoe-pairs.title: Shoe pairs
routine-shoe-pairs.goal: Match shoes, tell sizes apart and learn to leave them tidy.
materials: Family shoes, 3 or 4 pairs
steps: Mix the shoes up by the front door.
Ask: “Where is this shoe's partner?”
Let them place each pair together, side by side.
At the end, let them guess whose each pair is.
variants: Easier: use only two very different pairs.
Harder: let them line them up from biggest to smallest.
routine-shoe-pairs.safety: Use shoes without long laces, and set aside any with heels or buckles.
